stem.text: In plants and humans, the phenotype of an organism is determined by the genotype and the environment.
Plants from the genus Primula have different petal colours. The presence of the pigment malvidin results in blue petals.
The metabolic pathway for malvidin synthesis is controlled by gene T/t. The presence of the dominant allele T results in blue petals.

Another gene, gene D/d, at a different locus, also influences the malvidin synthesis pathway. When the dominant allele D is present, its gene product suppresses the malvidin synthesis pathway. This is summarised in Fig. 3.1.

stem.caption: Fig. 3.1
stem.alt: Two pathway diagrams. Top: precursor, with an arrow labelled allele T pointing to malvidin, then an arrow to blue petals. Bottom: precursor, with an arrow labelled allele D pointing to no malvidin, then an arrow to non-blue petals.

stem.text: A genetic cross was carried out between two plants heterozygous at both gene loci. The resulting offspring genotypes are shown in a Punnett square in Fig. 3.2.
State which of the genotypes shown in Fig. 3.2 have blue petals.

explanation.text: Blue petals need malvidin, which needs allele T present (Fig. 3.1) and no dominant D allele to suppress the pathway. Scanning the grid for genotypes with at least one T and no D (i.e. dd) gives TTdd (one cell) and Ttdd (two cells, both the same genotype).

reasoningChain: Blue petals require T present and D absent, i.e. T_dd.
Scan the 16-cell grid for T_dd genotypes: TTdd and Ttdd.

inferredMistakes.text: Including a tt dd genotype, overlooking that T itself (not just the absence of D) is required to make malvidin in the first place.

stem.text: State the ratio of non-blue to blue petals for the cross shown in Fig. 3.2.

explanation.text: Of the 16 genotypes in the grid, blue petals need at least one T allele and no D allele (dd): that is TTdd (once) and Ttdd (twice), 3 genotypes in total. The other 13 either have a D allele (suppressed) or are tt (no malvidin made). So the ratio is 13 non-blue : 3 blue.

reasoningChain: Count genotypes with at least one T and no D: TTdd, Ttdd, Ttdd = 3.

stem.text: Name the type of gene interaction that has caused the offspring ratio you have stated in (a)(ii).

explanation.text: Gene D/d masks the effect of gene T/t: whatever genotype is present at the T/t locus, a dominant D allele suppresses malvidin production and blocks blue petals. One gene's expression overriding another gene's phenotype at a different locus is epistasis.

reasoningChain: The 13:3 ratio (rather than a standard 9:3:3:1 dihybrid ratio) signals that one gene is masking the other.
This masking between two different loci is called epistasis.

stem.text: Gene T/t and gene D/d code for proteins that are involved in the control of the production of malvidin.
Discuss the possible roles of the proteins coded for by gene T/t and gene D/d in the control of the production of malvidin.

points.text: dominant allele / T / D, results in a functional protein ;
two recessive alleles / tt / dd, results in a non-functional protein ;
(so enzyme catalyses) production of, malvidin / pigment ;
(inhibitor) binds to enzyme (coded for by) gene T/t ;
(so) reaction to produce, malvidin / pigment, does not occur ;
protein (coded by T / t) could be a transcription factor ;
transcription factor allow the production of enzyme (needed in the metabolic pathway) ;
protein (coded by D/d) could cause the inhibition of transcription factor ;

explanation.text: The MS credits two alternative models of how these proteins could work, both consistent with Fig. 3.1. Model one: T codes for an enzyme that catalyses the precursor → malvidin step, and D codes for an inhibitor protein that binds that enzyme and blocks the reaction. Model two: T codes for a transcription factor that switches on the gene for the pathway's enzyme, and D codes for a protein that inhibits that transcription factor. In both models a dominant allele gives a working protein and two recessive alleles give a non-functional one, and in both D's product acts downstream of (blocks) T's product, matching the epistasis in (a)(iii).

reasoningChain: State the general rule: dominant allele → functional protein, double recessive → non-functional protein.
Propose one specific role for the T/t protein (enzyme or transcription factor).
Propose the matching role for the D/d protein that blocks or inhibits it.
Link back to why this gives epistasis: D's product can override T's regardless of T/t genotype.

inferredMistakes.text: Describing D/d as acting upstream of or independently from T/t, rather than specifically blocking/inhibiting the T/t product or pathway, which is what creates epistasis rather than simple independent gene action.

stem.text: Some humans have the inherited condition haemophilia.
Explain the relationship between the F8 gene, factor VIII and the condition haemophilia.

points.text: (so) blood does not clot quickly enough / excessive bleeding occurs (after an injury) ;
link the phenotype to the genotype ;

examples: e.g. prevents activation of thrombin / fibrinogen not converted to fibrin
different mutations cause a range of severity of haemophilia

explanation.text: The F8 gene is on the X chromosome and codes for the clotting protein factor VIII. The recessive allele produces non-functional (or no, or too little) factor VIII. Because blood clotting needs factor VIII, a person with two copies of the recessive allele (homozygous recessive female, or the only copy in a male) cannot clot blood quickly after an injury: this is haemophilia. Because the gene is X-linked, males (XfY) need only one recessive allele to be affected, while females need two (XfXf), which is why haemophilia is much more common in men.

reasoningChain: F8 gene (X-linked, recessive allele) → non-functional/absent factor VIII protein.
No functional factor VIII → blood clots too slowly → excessive bleeding = haemophilia.
Link genotype to phenotype using X<sup>F</sup>/X<sup>f</sup> notation, explaining why males are affected more often.

inferredMistakes.text: Describing haemophilia as caused directly by a faulty gene without mentioning the missing/non-functional protein (factor VIII) as the mechanism linking genotype to the bleeding phenotype.
